---
title: "Vertical events"
description: "How OPDI finds level flight, the top of climb and the top of descent, level-offs during climb and descent, and flight-level crossings. Not validated."
---

## What it is

These events describe the vertical profile of a flight: when it climbs, when it
flies level and when it descends. Four families are published.

**Level flight from the flight phases.** `level-start` and `level-end` mark the
start and the end of each period in which the aircraft flies level, cruise
included. A **cruise** is the long level part of a flight at its highest
altitude.

**Top of climb and top of descent.** `top-of-climb` marks the end of the climb
to cruise, and `top-of-descent` the start of the final descent. Both follow the
method that the EUROCONTROL Performance Review Unit (PRU) uses for its vertical
flight efficiency indicators. Their `info` field holds the top found before it
was moved (see below: `d200_time`, `d200_altitude_ft`), whether it was moved
(`relocated`), the analysis radius (`analysis_radius_nm`, 200) and `method`
(`pru`).

**Level-offs.** A level-off is a period of level flight during the climb or
the descent, below the cruise. Air traffic control often asks for one to
separate aircraft, and each one costs fuel. ICAO's vertical efficiency
indicators count them (KPI17 for the climb, KPI19 for the descent). OPDI
publishes each one as a pair of events: `level-off-climb-start` and
`level-off-climb-end`, `level-off-descent-start` and `level-off-descent-end`.
Their `info` holds the indicator (`kpi`), the duration (`duration_s`,
seconds), the distance flown (`distance_nm`, nautical miles) and the altitude
of the level-off (`level_ft`, feet).

**Flight-level crossings.** A **flight level** is an altitude in hundreds of
feet measured from the standard air pressure of 1013.25 hPa, as aircraft
altimeters show it at altitude: flight level 100 (FL100) is about 10,000 ft.
OPDI publishes every crossing of FL50, FL70, FL100 and FL245 as `xing-fl50`,
`xing-fl70`, `xing-fl100` and `xing-fl245`. Their `info` holds the number of
the crossing of that level on the flight (`crossing_seq`, 1 for the first),
the direction (`direction`: `up` or `down`) and the time between the two state
vectors the crossing was placed between (`bracket_s`, seconds).

All four families carry the version `events_v0.3.0`.

## How it is computed

All four work on the cleaned state vectors of each track (see
[Trajectory cleaning](trajectory-cleaning.qmd)), one every 5 seconds, using the
barometric altitude. Each works separately on each stretch of a track between
two reception gaps of more than 30 minutes (see
[Track identity](track-identity.qmd)), so nothing is computed across a gap.

### Level flight from the flight phases (`level-start`, `level-end`)

The flight phase of each state vector is decided by **fuzzy logic**, with the
rules and values of OpenAP, an open aircraft performance model. Each phase has
a rule that scores, between 0 and 1, how well the state vector fits it. A
rule combines three scores, one each for altitude, vertical rate and ground
speed, and keeps the lowest of the three:

| Phase | Altitude | Vertical rate | Ground speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ground | near the airport's elevation (score 0 from 200 ft above it) | near 0 ft/min | near 0 kt |
| Climb | around 10,000 ft (wide) | climbing (full score from 1,000 ft/min) | around 300 kt |
| Descent | around 10,000 ft (wide) | descending (full score from 1,000 ft/min) | around 300 kt |
| Cruise | around 35,000 ft (wide) | near 0 ft/min | around 600 kt |
| Level | around 10,000 ft (wide) | near 0 ft/min | around 300 kt |

1. The phase of a state vector is the one whose rule scores highest. A rule
   with a missing input is not used. If no rule can be used, the state vector
   has no phase.
2. Each state vector then takes the phase that is most common within 30 s
   before and after it (a 60 s window). On a tie it keeps its own phase. This
   removes single misclassified state vectors.
3. `level-start` is placed at a state vector in cruise or level flight whose
   previous state vector with a phase had another phase (or that has no such
   predecessor), and at the first cruise state vector of the track.
4. `level-end` is placed at a state vector in cruise or level flight whose
   next state vector with a phase has another phase (or that has no such
   successor), and at the last cruise state vector of the track.

The events take the position, altitude and measurements of their state vector.

### Level segments for the tops and the level-offs

The tops and the level-offs use a second, geometric definition of level
flight, from the PRU method:

1. Interpolate the altitude in a straight line onto a regular grid of one
   point every 10 s.
2. A grid point is **level** when the altitude stays within a band of 50 ft
   over the following 10 s. This is a vertical speed of at most 300 ft/min.
3. Consecutive level points form a **level segment**, which ends 10 s after its
   last level point. Its altitude is the mean altitude over the segment.
4. Segments shorter than 20 s are dropped.

### Top of climb and top of descent

1. For each state vector, compute the great-circle distance to the departure
   and destination airports of the flight list.
2. Find the first moment the aircraft is 200 NM or more from the departure
   airport. If it never is, use the end of the track. Find the last moment it
   is more than 200 NM from the destination airport. If it never is, use the
   start of the track.
3. **First estimate.** The top of climb is the first moment the aircraft
   reaches its highest altitude between the start of the track and the first
   moment found in step 2. The top of descent is the last moment it is at its
   highest altitude between the last moment found in step 2 and the end of the
   track.
4. **Move the top past a cruise step.** The **exclusion box** runs from the
   estimated top's altitude down to 90% of it. If a level segment inside the
   box lasts more than 300 s and begins before the estimated top of climb, it
   is cruise: the top of climb moves to the start of the first such segment,
   at that segment's altitude. The top of descent likewise moves to the end of
   the last such segment after it.
5. The event takes the position and measurements of the last state vector at
   or before its time.

### Level-offs

A level segment is a climb level-off when all of these hold:

- it ends before the top of climb;
- its altitude is at least 3,000 ft above the departure airport;
- it starts within 200 NM of the departure airport;
- it is not cruise: it is not both at or above 90% of the top of climb's
  altitude and longer than 300 s.

A level segment is a descent level-off under the mirror conditions: it starts
after the top of descent, its altitude is at least 1,800 ft above the
destination airport, it ends within 200 NM of the destination airport, and it
is not cruise. A flight needs both a top of climb and a top of descent to have
any level-off.

The start and end events take the altitude of the segment. They have no
position and no distance or time measurements; the segment's duration and
distance are in `info`.

### Flight-level crossings

1. For each of FL50, FL70, FL100 and FL245, follow the aircraft's flight level
   (barometric altitude divided by 100 ft).
2. To ignore small up and down movements around a level, a **dead band** of
   300 ft is used on each side of it. The aircraft counts as above FL100 only
   once it is above 10,300 ft, and as below only once it is below 9,700 ft.
   Inside the band it keeps the side it was last on. A crossing is the moment
   the side changes.
3. The time and position of the crossing are interpolated in a straight line
   between the two state vectors on either side of the level itself. The
   altitude of the event is exactly the level (10,000 ft for FL100).
4. Every crossing is kept, numbered in time order.

The same crossing method is used for the
[distance rings](distance-rings.qmd), with distance to the airport instead of
altitude.

## Reference data

None. No source available to OPDI records the top of climb, the top of
descent, level segments or flight-level crossings of individual flights. The
airport operator records used for the take-off and landing times hold nothing
about the climb, cruise or descent.

## Validation method

Not validated against reference data.

The code of the tops and of the level segments is tested on made-up
trajectories whose correct answer is known by construction, for example a
climb with a hold inside the exclusion box that must move the top, and the
same hold below the box that must not. These tests show that the rules work
as written. They do not show how well the rules describe real flights.

The crossing method used for the flight levels was compared with reference
data where it is applied to distance rings (see
[Distance rings](distance-rings.qmd#results)), which supports the
interpolation, but not the altitude data it is applied to here.

Validation would need, for the same flights, the tops and level segments
computed by an independent source, for example EUROCONTROL's own computation
of its vertical flight efficiency indicators from Network Manager trajectory
data, or flight data recorded on board.

## Limitations

- None of these events has been compared with reference data.
- `level-start`/`level-end` and the level-offs answer different questions and
  are not interchangeable. The first asks whether the state vector looks like
  level flight; the second whether the altitude stays inside a 50 ft band. For
  vertical efficiency indicators, use the level-offs.
- The phase rules use OpenAP's speeds: cruise is centred on 600 kt and climb
  and level flight on 300 kt. Turboprops and light aircraft fit these rules
  poorly, so their `level-start`/`level-end` are less reliable. The top of
  climb and top of descent do not depend on these rules.
- The tops are computed per track. A track that starts in the air or ends
  before landing can have its top at its first or last state vector.
- Without a departure (or destination) airport in the flight list, the 200 NM
  limit cannot be applied, and the whole track is used for the top. Such a
  flight has no level-offs at all.
- Level-off events have no position and no distance or time measurements.
  Their `distance_nm` in `info` is a difference of the distance flown and has
  the limits described in [Measurements](measurements.qmd).
- Barometric altitude is not corrected for the local air pressure. Flight
  levels are defined that way, so the crossings are right. The 3,000 ft and
  1,800 ft limits above the airports, however, are compared with uncorrected
  altitude, and move slightly with the weather.
- An aircraft that levels off within 300 ft of a monitored flight level never
  leaves the dead band, so that crossing is not reported. The level-off events
  describe that case.
- When the two state vectors around a crossing are far apart (see
  `bracket_s`), the interpolated time and position are uncertain.
- A level segment shorter than 20 s is not reported. The interpolation on a
  10 s grid smooths short changes of altitude.
